A1.justification: Both PDFs describe NV-Embed and contain matching architecture descriptions and original experiments. Their text, equations, figures, tables and appendices are readable and support reliable comparison.

before.justification: V1 reports original MTEB/BEIR evaluations and experiments comparing attention masks and pooling methods in Tables 1–4.

after.justification: V2 retains original experiments and adds NV-Embed-v2 results, training and data-curation ablations, AIR-Bench evaluations and an attention visualization.

M1.justification: Sections 4.1–4.3 introduce E5-Mistral positive-aware negative mining, replacing the earlier encoder-based/BM25 procedures, and use sampled examples instead of label texts for selected multiclass and clustering tasks. V2 also adds Mixtral synthetic-data generation and STS document-side instructions. The latent-attention architecture and two-stage training framework remain.

E1.justification: V2 retains the 56-task MTEB evaluation but adds AIR-Bench evaluation on eight English QA and fifteen long-document datasets, including law and book domains. Training expands through additional retrieval, classification and clustering datasets and 120,000 synthetic examples spanning 60,000 tasks (Sections 4.1–4.3 and Appendix A).

E2.justification: Table 1 adds Bge-en-icl, Stella-1.5B-v5, SFR-Embedding-2R, Gte-Qwen2-7B-instruct and Bge-multilingual-gemma2, while removing Gte-Qwen1.5, Voyage-lite, Google-gecko and LLM2Vec from that comparison. The detailed per-dataset comparator set also changes, and AIR-Bench comparisons introduce Linq-Embed-Mistral.

E3.justification: Reported warm-up steps change from 500 to 50. Training sample counts change substantially, including NLI from 20k to 270k and PAQ from 100k to 500k, and several training/evaluation instructions change. V2 introduces single-stage/reversed-stage controls and AIR-Bench protocols using nDCG@10 and Recall@10. The reported sequence limit, batch size and stage budgets remain unchanged.

E4.justification: The original attention/pooling ablations survive in v2 Table 2. New analyses test single-stage versus two-stage and reversed-stage training, label-based versus example-based supervision, and incremental effects of negative mining, additional public data and synthetic data (Tables 3–5). Appendix C adds a review-sentiment latent-attention case study, and Appendix A examines out-of-domain generalization.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals, error bars or statistical significance tests. The added experiments continue the existing point-estimate reporting practice.

E6.justification: V2 retains NV-Embed-v1's 69.32 MTEB and 59.36 retrieval scores and adds NV-Embed-v2 scores of 72.31 and 62.65 under revised training and instructions. These are distinct model configurations, not an isolated same-setting architectural gain. New ablation and AIR-Bench results include 52.28 QA and 74.78 long-document averages. Some original per-dataset baseline and ablation entries are replaced in Table 11.

T1.justification: Section 4.1.1 newly defines the negative-score cutoff as the positive score multiplied by a percentage margin, set to 0.95. This is a limited mathematical selection-rule addition. The latent-attention equation and associated definitions remain unchanged, and neither version contains theoretical guarantees or proofs.

C1.justification: V1 emphasizes achieving leading results without synthetic data. V2 makes data curation, including synthetic generation and example-based labeling, an explicit contribution and claims sustained leadership across two model releases. It also adds claims of leading clustering/classification performance and generalization to AIR-Bench, extending the original MTEB-centered contribution.

C2.justification: V2 adds interpretations of reversed-stage training trade-offs and latent specialization for review sentiment. Appendix A argues that MTEB improvements need not transfer to out-of-domain retrieval, illustrating this with the SFR models, while interpreting NV-Embed's AIR-Bench results as generalization evidence. These extend the earlier pooling and attention explanations.

D1.justification: V2 documents the mining teacher and cutoff, synthetic generator and prompt templates, uniform training-data sampling, and optimizer restarts between stages. Training counts and instruction tables are revised and expanded. The abstract changes from promising an NV-Embed-v1 release to reporting an NV-Embed-v2 release with a different model link; actual external availability is not established by the PDFs.

R1.justification: Section 2.2 expands positioning around data curation and reproducibility, discussing Linq-Embed, explicitly adopting NV-Retriever's mining technique, and contrasting Bge-en-icl's few-shot training with zero-shot evaluation. It also discusses newer competitors' limited disclosure and adds references supporting the expanded datasets and methods.

P1.justification: The main section sequence and much of the architecture and training exposition remain intact. V2 revises the abstract, contribution list and conclusion, adds data-curation and ablation subsections, expands the appendix organization and adds acknowledgments. These are targeted narrative revisions accompanying the scientific additions.

P2.justification: V1 Tables 2–3 are merged into v2 Table 2. V2 adds several ablation and AIR-Bench tables, synthetic-generation prompt tables and the attention heatmap in Figure 2. The detailed benchmark table moves to the appendix with substantially different columns, and the document adopts ICLR formatting. Figure 1 remains materially unchanged.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially strengthens evidence for the training recipe: Tables 4–5 directly test training order and data-curation choices that v1 did not isolate, while AIR-Bench adds generalization evidence beyond MTEB. Expanded procedural documentation also improves reproducibility. These gains outweigh reduced per-dataset ablation detail and documentation errors, notably Table 9's Medrxiv instructions for Reddit/StackExchange. Uncertainty reporting remains absent, limiting confidence in small score differences.
